title: My Grandfather Left Me Flaking Wooden Ducks Instead of Cash or Land

blocks.text: The reading took twenty minutes in a small paneled office behind the county courthouse. My brother, Greg, sat on the leather sofa with his car keys already in his hand. My sister, Denise, had her checkbook balanced on her knee like she was ready to deposit something before noon.
Grandpa Donald had been gone three weeks. He was eighty-eight, worked forty-two years at the grain elevator in town, and lived in the small cedar cabin out on Black Lake.
When the lawyer, Mr. Vance, adjusted his glasses and unfolded the will, nobody looked at each other.
The lake cabin and the four wooded acres went directly to Greg. Greg didn’t even blink. He just nodded, slipped his keys into his pocket, and leaned back.
The bank accounts, totaling just under ninety-one thousand dollars after final medical bills, went entirely to Denise. Denise let out a small, quiet breath and made a neat mark on her legal pad.
Then Mr. Vance looked down at the last paragraph.
“To my granddaughter, Sarah,” Mr. Vance read, “I leave the rough-pine storage crate currently kept under the workbench in the back shed, containing my collection of hand-carved waterfowl decoys.”
That was it. No savings bonds. No share in the cabin. Not even a mention of his truck, which had already been sold to cover his funeral costs.
Greg laughed under his breath as we walked down the brick steps outside into the muggy July heat. “Well, Sarah, you always were the sentimental one.
They were his pets, basically. He sat out in that freezing shed whittling them for forty years instead of watching the ball game.”

“Are you going to keep them in your apartment?” Denise asked. She wasn’t being mean, just practical in that distant way she always had. “Because if you don’t have room, you can leave them out by the shed door when Greg clears the place out. Someone might pick them up for firewood.”

My pride wouldn’t let me leave them behind. Grandpa had raised the three of us for four years after our mother died, before our dad remarried and moved us two towns over. I remembered the cedar shavings on his wool socks and the smell of boiled linseed oil on his hands when he made us oatmeal before school.
I drove my beat-up 2008 Chevy Impala out to the cabin that evening before Greg started hauling trash.
The crate was under the back bench, covered in grey sawdust and spiderwebs. It was heavy, made of rough-sawn pine planks with rope handles. Inside were twelve wooden birds.

They weren’t shiny or polished. The paint was dull, chipped, and flaking away around the bills and tails. Two of them had small lead weights tacked to their flat bottoms with rusted square-headed nails. To anyone looking into that box, it was just a pile of dusty, battered yard decorations.
I hauled the crate into my spare bedroom and went back to work at the county clinic the next morning. I figured eventually I would scrub them down and set a couple on my back porch railing.
Two months later, in late September, the transmission on my Impala gave out at a red light on Route 6.
The tow truck driver hauled it into Miller’s Auto, and Pete Miller called me two hours later with the bad news.
The second-gear clutch band had snapped clean. He could put in a rebuilt transmission from a salvage yard for seven hundred dollars, parts and labor.

Seven hundred dollars might as well have been seven thousand. My checking account had eighty-four dollars in it, and rent was due in ten days. I worked thirty-two hours a week doing patient intake, and every spare dollar went straight to groceries and my own heating oil bill.
I sat on the edge of my bed that night, looking across the hall at the open door of the spare bedroom. The pine crate was sitting right where I had left it.

I walked in, reached down, and lifted out the duck that sat on top. It was a canvasback drake with a worn reddish-brown head and a wide, grey back. The paint on the neck had spider-webbed into tiny cracks, and there was a shallow dent near the tail feathers where it had bumped against something hard years ago.
I thought maybe someone who decorated lake houses would give me fifty or seventy-five dollars for it. Even fifty dollars would buy a week of groceries while I figured out how to pay Pete for the car.
The next afternoon, on my lunch break, I wrapped the wooden bird in an old yellow bath towel and drove Pete’s loaner truck out to Halloran’s Antiques on the highway edge of town.

Mr. Halloran was in his seventies, wearing a blue cardigan with worn elbows and reading a catalog behind a high counter piled with brass lamps and old pocket watches. The bell above the door jangled when I walked in.
“Afternoon,” he said without looking all the way up. “Looking for something specific?”

“No, sir,” I said, setting the bundle on the counter. “I was actually wondering if you bought old hunting gear. My grandfather passed away, and he left me a box of old wooden ducks he made. I’m having car trouble, and I just need to see if one might be worth something.”
The heavy wooden duck sat there on the polished oak counter under the fluorescent bulb.
Mr. Halloran pushed his reading glasses up on his forehead, then pulled a pair of stronger bifocals from his shirt pocket. He didn’t say a word. He reached out with both hands and lifted the duck.
He didn’t look at the paint first. He turned the bird upside down in his palms, bringing the flat, weighted bottom right up to his face.
The shop went completely silent except for the hum of an old refrigerator in the back room.
Mr. Halloran’s hands stopped moving. He held the duck dead still for ten full seconds. Then his thumb moved slowly over the wood near the lead keel weight, brushing away a smudge of dry mud.
My chest tightened. I thought he was about to tell me the wood had dry rot and wasn’t worth five dollars.
He set the bird down on the counter with extraordinary care, like it was made of blown glass. When he looked up at me, his face was pale, and his voice dropped to a near whisper.
“Ma’am,” he said, looking straight into my eyes, “do you actually know who carved this?”
“My grandfather,” I stammered, feeling foolish. “Donald Miller. He had a workshop out by Black Lake. He whittled out there in the evenings.”
Mr. Halloran shook his head very slowly.
“Your grandfather didn’t carve this,” he said quietly. “Look right here.”
Mr. Halloran took a small magnifying loop from his pocket and pointed with the tip of an unsharpened pencil at the wood near the keel.
Burned faintly into the pine, almost hidden beneath sixty years of river grime and dried swamp mud, was a clean mark shaped like an anchor with two tiny capital letters stamped beneath it: C.P.

“Charles Perdew,” Mr. Halloran said, his voice flat with absolute certainty. “Illinois River. Henry, Illinois. Early 1920s. This isn’t whittling, young lady. This is one of the finest hollow-carved canvasbacks to survive outside of a private museum.”
I stared at him, my mouth slightly open. “A museum? But it’s chipped. The paint is coming off.”

“That’s original paint,” he said, his eyes practically locked to the bird. “If somebody had repainted it, it would be worth four hundred dollars. Because nobody touched it, because it was hunted over and put away dry in a dark box… this single bird will bring twelve to fifteen thousand dollars at a catalog auction in Chicago.”
The air went right out of my lungs. The counter seemed to tilt beneath my hands.
“Easily,” he replied. “And you said you have a box of them? How many?”
“Twelve,” I said, the word barely making it past my lips. “There are twelve birds in the crate.”

Mr. Halloran pulled his hands back from the counter and looked at me sternly over his glasses. “Pack this bird back in that towel right now. Don’t touch the surface with bare, oily fingers if you can avoid it. Go straight home, lock your door, and don’t clean them. Don’t use soap, don’t use wax, don’t wipe them with water. Call Guyette and Deeter or Copley Fine Art Auctions in Boston. Tell them what you have. Do not sell these to a local picker for gas money.”
I drove back to my apartment with both hands locked white-knuckle on the steering wheel of Pete’s loaner truck. My mind was spinning backward through thirty years of memories.
Why would Grandpa have those? He worked for an hourly wage at the grain elevator. He never hunted rich private clubs. He drove fifteen-year-old pickups and patched his boots with shoe glue.

When I got home, I locked the front door behind me. I brought the heavy pine crate into the middle of my small living room, set down a clean white bedsheet, and lifted the remaining eleven birds out one by one.
Under the strong floor lamp, I examined every single base.

They weren’t all the same maker. Four carried the burned anchor of Charles Perdew. Three had the crisp, stamped name of the Mason Decoy Factory, Premier Grade, with glass eyes that looked like wet amber. Two were flat-bottomed black ducks signed with initials cut deep into the wood with a knife: A.E.C. for Nathan Cobb Jr. from Virginia.
And tucked into the very bottom of the crate, resting flat between two old cedar shims, was a yellowed legal envelope folded in thirds.
My fingers were shaking as I pulled the paper out.
It was a handwritten letter on yellow legal paper, dated October 14, 1974. The handwriting was unmistakably my grandfather’s, written in firm, slanting ballpoint pen.
“To whoever opens this crate after I am gone,” it began.
“If Greg is reading this, you didn’t listen to a word I said about patience. If Denise is reading this, you were already counting the interest before the dirt settled.

“In the fall of 1958, a lawyer from Chicago named Harrington brought his son up to Black Lake for three weeks of mallard shooting. His car broke down on the logging trail, and his boy got double pneumonia in the rain. I carried that boy two miles out to the state road on my back and kept their fire lit until the county doctor arrived.
